item.description: Traditional midwives like Roberta Devers could be key to increasing vaccination as outbreaks spread in rural communities such as those in Pennsylvania.

media:content.media:text: A diptych.
Roberta Devers takes the blood pressure of Hannah Garman during a prenatal visit in Lititz, Penn., on Oct. 26, 2026.
media:content.media:description: Roberta Devers takes the blood pressure of Hannah Garman during a prenatal visit in Lititz, Penn., on Oct. 26, 2026.

media:content.media:text: Roberta Devers.
media:content.media:description: Devers said pregnant women with measles are having miscarriages. "While our Amish families believe God is always in control, they're emotional people, and like anyone else, they grieve the loss of a baby," Devers said.

media:content.media:text: Members of the amish community ride in a horse drawn carriage.
media:content.media:description: Members of the Amish community ride in a horse-drawn carriage in Lancaster, Pa., on Oct. 25. Many unvaccinated Amish people are asking for the shot as the outbreak continues.

media:content.media:text: A diptych.
media:content.media:description: Lancaster County, Pa., is home to the country's largest population of Amish people. About half have home births and largely rely on their nurse midwives for health advice.

media:content.media:text: A diptych.
media:content.media:description: Every day is laundry day in the heart of Amish country in rural Lancaster County. The family who lives here recently had measles.

media:content.media:text: A farm.
media:content.media:description: A farm in Lancaster County on Oct. 25. Experts worry that measles spread will continue now that the traditional Amish wedding season has begun.

media:content.media:text: Hannah Garman.
media:content.media:description: Garman, 27, is due with her third baby in early December. She was never vaccinated as a child and remains unprotected against measles as it spreads in Lancaster County.

media:content.media:text: Roberta Devers during a prenatal visit.
media:content.media:description: Nearly 100 women in Pennsylvania have had measles while pregnant. The virus can increase the risk for early birth and miscarriage.

media:content.media:text: Members of the amish community farm.
media:content.media:description: Members of the Amish community farm in Lancaster County on Oct. 26.

media:content.media:text: Roberta Devers speaks with a patient.
media:content.media:description: Devers speaks with a patient during a prenatal visit in Lancaster on Oct. 26.

media:content.media:text: Roberta Devers.
media:content.media:description: Roberta Devers arrives for a prenatal visit in Lititz on Oct. 26.

item.title: She’s delivered 2,000 babies. The measles outbreak changed her mind about vaccines.
